assumptions: Input is a mutable sequence with O(1) indexed reads/writes. Element comparisons are O(1). Exclude the input and returned sequence.
input_size: n = len(collection); assume comparison of two elements is O(1).
rationale: Time: The outer loop runs n-1 times and the inner scan examines the remaining suffix. The total comparisons are (n-1)+(n-2)+...+1 = Θ(n²), independent of input order. Auxiliary space: The algorithm sorts the input sequence in place and uses only a fixed number of index variables and one temporary swap value. Owner review: Confirmed against source: the outer loop runs n−1 times and the inner scan examines each remaining suffix, producing (n−1)+(n−2)+…+1 = Θ(n²) comparisons for every input order. The in-place swaps use only fixed scalar state, so auxiliary space is O(1).

assumptions: Start with index=0, number_of_items=n, max_weight>=0, and valid weights/values lists. Treat integer operations and list indexing as O(1). The exponential label is the worst case (for example, capacity is at least the sum of all nonnegative item weights); pruning can reduce work on other inputs.
input_size: n = number_of_items; weights and values each contain at least n entries.
rationale: Time: For each item, the function always explores the exclude branch and explores the include branch when it fits. When all include branches remain feasible, the recursion tree has 2^n leaves; work per node is constant. Auxiliary space: The recursion advances index by one on every call, so the deepest call chain has at most n+1 frames. No memoization table is allocated. Owner review: Confirmed against source: there is no memoization or table. The exclude branch always recurses and the include branch recurses when the item fits, giving O(2ⁿ) worst-case calls when all branches remain feasible. The recursion depth is at most n+1, so auxiliary space is O(n).

assumptions: Analyze merge_sort on a list of comparable values with O(1) comparisons. Python list pop(0) shifts the remaining references and costs O(k) for a list of length k. Exclude the input and returned list from auxiliary space; count recursive slices and intermediate merge lists.
expected_auxiliary_space_exact: O(n) excluding input and returned list
input_size: n = len(collection); assume element comparisons are O(1).
rationale: Owner-reviewed time and auxiliary-space rationale: The labels remain O(n²) time and O(n) auxiliary space; this revision corrects assumptions and rationale only. In a merge of two non-empty halves, one half is eventually exhausted by repeated pop(0) calls. The shifts from removing all elements of that half sum to Θ(n²) for the top-level merge regardless of input order, so T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n²)=Θ(n²). Excluding input and returned output, recursion slices and intermediate lists use O(n) peak auxiliary storage. The source docstring says O(n log n), but that claim omits list.pop(0) shifting costs.

assumptions: Both strings are non-null. For the proposed coarse n² scoring class, analyze non-empty strings and set n=max(m,k) and assume m and k are of comparable order; the exact two-parameter bound is O(mk), not necessarily Θ(n²) when lengths are highly unbalanced. Java string splitting and character comparisons are assumed linear/constant per character respectively.
input_size: m = str1.length(), k = str2.length(); coarse n = max(m,k).
rationale: For non-empty strings, the DP fills the (m+1)×(k+1) table, giving Θ(mk) time and auxiliary space. StringBuilder reconstruction and backtracking take O(m+k), dominated by the table fill. Null or empty input returns before table allocation. The coarse O(n²) class uses n=max(m,k) and is tight when m and k are comparable.

assumptions: Analyze the full public find call, including isSorted, not just the search loop. Array is non-null and indexed access and Comparable.compareTo are O(1). An empty array is rejected in O(1). The imported SearchAlgorithm interface only declares the method contract.
input_size: n = array.length; array is required to be sorted.
rationale: Time: Before its Fibonacci-search loop, find calls isSorted, which scans adjacent array elements and takes O(n). The subsequent Fibonacci search takes O(log n), so total method time remains O(n). Auxiliary space: Both sortedness validation and Fibonacci search keep only a fixed number of indices and Fibonacci counters; no size-dependent storage or recursion is used. Owner review: Confirmed against source: the public find call first performs a plain adjacent-pair sortedness scan in O(n), then runs the Fibonacci search in O(log n). The validation dominates, so full-call time is O(n). Both loops use only scalar indices and Fibonacci counters, so auxiliary space is O(1). The class Javadoc describes the search loop alone and omits validation.
